pos: n. (the Rhine city of the great presses, reformed under Oecolampadius in 1529, and the printing house and asylum of Reformation Europe)
etymology: Latin Basilea, from the Greek basileia, a royal place, the Roman Basilia on the Rhine; German Basel, French Bâle.
biblical_def: Basel is the Swiss city whose presses mattered more than its politics. Standing where the Rhine turns north, with a university from 1460 and the greatest printing houses north of Venice, it published Erasmus's Greek New Testament at Froben's press in 1516, the text from which Luther and Tyndale translated; Erasmus himself lived and died there. Johannes Oecolampadius, preaching from 1522, led the Reformation to its conclusion in February 1529, when the guilds forced the council's hand, the images were taken out of the minster, and the mass was abolished; the Basel Confession of 1534 followed, and the First Helvetic Confession was drafted there in 1536. The city then became an asylum. Italians fleeing the Roman inquisition, French fleeing the Valois, and Englishmen fleeing Mary all found houses and work in Basel, and its printers put out what no other city would, including Castellio's arguments against the burning of heretics. The dictionary enters Basel because the two things it gave the Reformation were a Greek text and a refuge, and because it is the one Reformed city that kept printing the men the Reformed authorities elsewhere wanted silenced.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a press as the business of printing; an asylum as a place of refuge; a minster as the church of a monastery; and a guild as an incorporated society of tradesmen.
webster_full: PRESS, n. A machine for printing; the art or business of printing and publishing; the printing house itself.
ASYLUM, n. A sanctuary or place of refuge; any place of retreat and security.
MINSTER, n. A monastery; an ecclesiastical convent or fraternity; a cathedral church.
GUILD, n. A society, fraternity or corporation, associated for some common purpose, as of trade.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge of the moral quality of actions.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.
Rom 14:4
Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.
corruption_summary: Rhine city of the Froben press and Erasmus's Greek New Testament, reformed under Oecolampadius in 1529, and the asylum and printing house of Reformation Europe.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the execution of men for their doctrine by Protestant magistrates, and Basel is where it was first argued against in print. Sebastian Castellio, professor of Greek there, published after Servetus's burning at Geneva in 1553 the treatise asking whether heretics are to be persecuted, and answered that they are not; the dictionary holds Servetus's denial of the Trinity to be a damning error and holds that Geneva was wrong to burn him, and records that Castellio, whose own views of Scripture and of free will the dictionary does not share, was right on this point. The parable of the tares is to the purpose, where the householder forbids the uprooting, “lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them” (Mat 13:29).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the instrument given the church against error is the word, which is sharper than any magistrate's sentence: “the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12). The caution about judging another man's servant stands over the whole quarrel, “Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?” (Rom 14:4). Basel's real weapon was its presses, and the promise over that work is that the word “shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).

pos: n. (the Three Leagues of the eastern Alps, German Graubünden, reformed by the Ilanz articles and the first land to have Scripture in Romansh)
etymology: French Grisons, from the Grey League, German Graubunden, the grey leagues, for the undyed homespun of its peasants; Romansh Grischun.
biblical_def: The Grisons were a federation of three leagues of Alpine valleys, allied to the Swiss but not a canton, governed by the votes of its communes, and that constitution shaped its Reformation. The Articles of Ilanz, agreed by the leagues in 1524 and extended in 1526, did not establish a religion; they subjected the clergy to civil courts, forbade appeals to foreign bishops, required that preaching be from Scripture, and then left each commune free to choose its own faith by its own vote. The result was a permanently mixed country, parish by parish, with Reformed and Catholic valleys side by side. Johannes Comander at Chur and Philipp Gallicius organised the Reformed side, the synod of Chur governed it, and the leagues' Romansh-speaking communes received Scripture in their own tongue, Jachiam Bifrun printing the New Testament in Ladin in 1560. The leagues also ruled the Italian-speaking Valtellina as subject territory, where in July 1620 the Catholic party massacred several hundred Protestants in what is called the Sacro Macello, and the Thirty Years War then came through the passes. The dictionary enters the Grisons because a commune-by-commune vote is the nearest thing in the Reformation to a settlement by consent, and it produced neither uniformity nor peace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a league as a confederacy; a commune as a small territorial district; a pass as a narrow passage through mountains; and a massacre as the murder of many with cruelty.
webster_full: LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.
COMMUNE, n. A small territorial district in some European countries, with its own local government.
PASS, n. A narrow passage, entrance or avenue; a narrow or difficult place of entrance and exit, as a defile.
MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers, with cruelty or atrocity.
SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.

Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.

Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Isa 8:20

corruption_summary: Three Leagues of the eastern Alps whose Ilanz articles of 1524 left each commune to choose its faith, and where the Valtellina massacre of 1620 killed several hundred Protestants.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the massacre done for religion, and the Grisons carry one of the worst in the Alps. In July 1620 the Catholic party of the Valtellina, the leagues' Italian-speaking subject valley, killed several hundred of their Protestant neighbours over some days; the dictionary names it plainly and also names the provocation, which was years of Grisons rule imposed by a foreign-speaking Protestant federation on a Catholic population it governed as subjects rather than as members. Neither fact excuses the other. The company under the altar is drawn from both sides of many such quarrels, those “slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) being counted by God and not by us.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that preaching from the text, which Ilanz required of every minister in the leagues, is a better foundation than a uniform settlement imposed from a capital. “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) was written into the articles themselves. The leagues also did the translator's work for a tongue almost nobody spoke, so that Romansh shepherds in the high valleys could “hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11), among rocks where “The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats” (Psa 104:18).

pos: n. (the Pays de Vaud, conquered by Bern from Savoy in 1536 and reformed by the Lausanne disputation, where Calvin first spoke in public)
etymology: French Vaud, from the Germanic Wald, a forest, through Latin Waldensis pagus; the Pays de Vaud lies along the north shore of Lake Geneva.
biblical_def: Vaud is the French-speaking country that Bern took by arms and reformed by argument. Savoy had held it; Bern conquered it in the winter and spring of 1536 and, instead of simply decreeing the Reformation, summoned a public disputation at Lausanne for the first week of October 1536, where William Farel and Pierre Viret led the Reformed side against the clergy of the diocese and the doctors of the Sorbonne's party. It was at Lausanne that a young Frenchman lately arrived in Geneva, John Calvin, rose and answered a charge that the Reformed despised the fathers by citing Tertullian, Chrysostom and Augustine from memory at length, which was his first public appearance in the Swiss Reformation. The disputation concluded for the Reformed, the mass was abolished across the Pays, and Bern founded the academy at Lausanne in 1537, where Viret and Theodore Beza taught. It ended badly: Viret and his colleagues held that a congregation must be able to exclude the scandalous from the Supper, Bern held that discipline belonged to its own council, and in 1559 Bern expelled them. They went to Geneva, and Beza became the first rector of Calvin's academy there. The dictionary enters Vaud because Bern's refusal of church discipline furnished Geneva with its best man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a disputation as a contest by arguments; an academy as a school of learning; excommunication as the act of ejecting from communion; and a rector as the head of a school.
webster_full: DISPUTATION, n. A contest in words or by arguments; a public exercise in argumentation, as before a council.
ACADEMY, n. A school or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school.
EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from the communion of the faithful.
RECTOR, n. The chief elective officer of some universities; the master of a school.
CONQUEST, n. The act of conquering; the subjection of a country or people by arms.
scriptures: But them that are without God judgeth. Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: French-speaking country taken by Bern from Savoy in 1536 and reformed by the Lausanne disputation, whose ministers Bern expelled in 1559 over church discipline.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the magistrate's seizure of the keys, and Vaud is where it cost the most. Bern's doctrine was Reformed and its council was pious, and it held that admission to and exclusion from the Lord's table was a civil administrative matter. The Lord gave that judgement to the congregation: “tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican” (Mat 18:17), and the apostolic command over a scandalous member is addressed to the body, “Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (1Co 5:13).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the self-examination and the oversight that together guard the table. The communicant is told “let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread” (1Co 11:28), and the officers are charged by the Holy Ghost to “feed the church of God” (Act 20:28). Bern took the second half into its own hands and lost Viret and Beza in 1559 for it, and the dictionary notes the irony without pretending it was providence excusing Bern: Geneva's academy opened because Lausanne's teachers were turned out.

pos: n. (the upper Rhone valley, where a Reformed minority was given the choice of recanting or emigrating and chose to go)
etymology: French Valais, German Wallis, from Latin vallis Poenina, the Pennine valley; the canton follows the upper Rhone to Lake Geneva.
biblical_def: Valais is the Alpine canton where the Reformation gained a real foothold and was removed by law a lifetime later. The upper Rhone valley was governed jointly by the bishop of Sion and the seven tithings of the Upper Valais, and from the 1520s evangelical books and preachers came up from Bern and Basel; by the later sixteenth century a substantial minority in the chief towns, Sion, Leuk and Visp among them, and a part of the governing families, were Reformed, and the diet more than once protected them against the bishop. The settlement came in 1603 and the years after: the diet, under pressure from the bishop, the Catholic cantons and the nuncio, resolved that the canton would be Catholic, and the Reformed were required to conform or to sell their property and leave. Most of the leading families left, chiefly for Bern and the Vaud. The Valais produced in Thomas Platter a boy who went out of these valleys as a goatherd, learned Hebrew, and became a printer and schoolmaster at Basel, whose autobiography is one of the plainest accounts we have of what the Reformation looked like from the bottom. The dictionary enters Valais because the choice offered in 1603 is the one offered to Protestants in a dozen Catholic states, and because most of them took the same answer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to recant as to retract an opinion; a tithing as a district or company of ten householders; a nuncio as a papal ambassador; and a goatherd as one who tends goats.
webster_full: RECANT, v. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to unsay what has been said.
TITHING, n. A district, township or parish subject to tithes; formerly a company of ten householders.
NUNCIO, n. An ambassador from the pope to some prince or state; a messenger.
GOATHERD, n. One whose occupation is to tend goats.
CONFORM, v. To comply with or yield obedience to; to make like in manners or opinions.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven.
For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance.

And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.
corruption_summary: Upper Rhone canton where a Reformed minority was protected by the diet and then required in 1603 to conform or to sell up and emigrate.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the recantation extorted by the threat of ruin, which is the commonest form persecution takes and the least dramatic. Nobody in Valais in 1603 was asked to walk to a stake; the Reformed families were asked to attend mass or to sell their land and go, and most of them sold. The Lord's warning makes the choice what it is: “whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:33), and a signature at a notary's table is a denial before men as truly as a word at an assize.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the willing loss of goods, which Scripture treats as a thing to be done cheerfully. Of the Hebrew Christians it is written that they “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods” (Heb 10:34), knowing of a better substance; and the promise is explicit that a man who has “forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother” (Mat 19:29) for Christ's sake shall receive manifold more. Those who went out of these valleys with what they could carry belong among the people “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38).

pos: n. (the Swiss common lordship where the Peace of Kappel left Reformed and Catholic sharing the same parish churches)
etymology: German Thurgau, the district of the river Thur; a common lordship of the Swiss cantons before it became a canton in 1803.
biblical_def: Thurgau is where the Swiss Reformation's stalemate was written into the furniture of the churches. It was not a canton but a common lordship, governed jointly by seven or eight cantons which after 1531 were divided between the Reformed and the Catholic sides, and neither bloc could impose its religion on a territory the other half-owned. The Second Peace of Kappel, concluded in November 1531 after Zwingli's death in the field, settled the common lordships by parity: each parish kept whatever it then had, Catholic worship was restored where it had been abolished, and in a large number of Thurgau parishes both communions were to use the same building, the Reformed holding the nave and the Catholics keeping the choir, often with a screen or rail between and the two services at different hours. Many of these shared churches are still shared. The dictionary enters Thurgau because the arrangement is the plainest monument in Europe to a reformation that was stopped short, and because the people in those parishes had to live as neighbours with men they believed to be in grave error, and mostly did.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines parity as equality; a nave as the body of a church; a choir as the part of a church where the singers sit; and a lordship as the territory of a lord.
webster_full: PARITY, n. Equality; as a parity of reasoning; equality of condition or of rank.
NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the balluster or railing of the door to the chief choir.
CHOIR, n. A band or collection of singers; the part of a church appropriated to the singers.
LORDSHIP, n. The state or quality of being a lord; the seigniory or domain of a lord.
PARTITION, n. That by which separate parts are made; a wall or division which separates one part from another.
scriptures: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another.
Mat 5:9
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
corruption_summary: Swiss common lordship where the Second Peace of Kappel of 1531 established parity, leaving many parishes with Reformed and Catholic worship in one shared church.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the pretence that such a settlement is agreement. Parity in Thurgau was not an ecumenical achievement but a truce between cantons that had just fought a war and could not win another, and the dictionary does not call a shared roof a shared faith; the two services taught contrary doctrines of the mass in the same building on the same morning. What can be said for it is that it stopped the killing and left the preaching free on both sides of the screen, and “live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18) is an apostolic command that a truce can serve.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the pursuit of peace is a positive duty and not merely the absence of a quarrel: “Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace” (Rom 14:19). The dictionary applies the apostle's word about the esteeming of days in its own place, that “every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5), to the manner of living alongside a neighbour in error, and not to the error itself. Over four centuries of Thurgau parishioners who managed it, the word stands: “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Mat 5:9).

“Blessed are the peacemakers” (Mat 5:9) — shared parish churches still shared after four centuries.

pos: n. (the Swiss district of the Baden disputation of 1526 and the Zofingen disputation of 1532, where the Reformation argued with Rome and then with the Anabaptists)
etymology: German Aargau, the district of the river Aare; partly Bernese territory and partly a common lordship before it became a canton in 1803.
biblical_def: Aargau is the Swiss country in which two of the Reformation's set-piece debates were held, and the pair of them show the movement arguing on both of its fronts. At Baden in May and June 1526 the Catholic cantons convened a disputation: Johann Eck and Johann Faber for Rome, Oecolampadius for the Reformed, with Zwingli refusing to attend on the ground that he would not be safe, and the Catholic majority declared itself the winner and used the verdict to press the Reformed cantons. At Zofingen in July 1532 the Bernese authorities convened a different disputation, between their own Reformed ministers and the Anabaptists of the region, over baptism, the oath, the magistracy, the ban and whether a church may contain the unregenerate; it ran for days, was recorded at length, and ended with the Anabaptists unpersuaded and afterwards punished. The dictionary enters Aargau because the Reformed at Baden asked for a hearing and did not get a fair one, and at Zofingen granted a hearing and then did not accept its implication. The second is the heavier charge, and it is ours.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a disputation as a contest by arguments; the ban as a public excommunication; an oath as a solemn affirmation with an appeal to God; and regeneration as the new birth.
webster_full: DISPUTATION, n. A contest in words or by arguments; a public exercise in argumentation, as in the schools.
BAN, n. A public proclamation; a curse or excommunication with curses; interdiction.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
REGENERATION, n. New birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God are subdued.
HEARING, n. The act of perceiving sound; audience; attention to what is delivered; judicial trial.
scriptures: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Jam 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
corruption_summary: Swiss district of the Baden disputation of 1526 against Rome and the Zofingen disputation of 1532 against the Anabaptists, convened by the Bernese authorities.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the disputation held with the verdict already decided, and the dictionary charges it to both sides in Aargau. Baden in 1526 was convened by men who meant to condemn and who kept the records; Zofingen in 1532 was convened by Reformed magistrates who heard the Anabaptists out at length and then fined, imprisoned and banished them for continuing to hold what they had not been answered on. The proverb is against both: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the hearing of the other side before judgement, which Scripture states as a rule of court: “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17). The Berean temper is the one wanted, of men who “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) when a new teaching was put to them. The apostolic order of speech is the practical form of it: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath” (Jam 1:19).

“He that is first in his own cause seemeth just” (Pro 18:17) — Zofingen, July 1532, and the punishments after it.
“let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath” (Jam 1:19) — a hearing granted and its implication refused.

pos: n. (the Swiss city-state that stayed Catholic between Bern and Geneva, expelled its Reformed, and buried Peter Canisius)
etymology: French Fribourg, German Freiburg, the free town, founded by Berthold IV of Zahringen in 1157 on the Sarine.
biblical_def: Fribourg is the Swiss city that did not reform, and its position made that decision matter far beyond its size. Standing on the language border between German and French and geographically between Bern and Geneva, it had been allied with Bern and Savoy and had a share in the common lordships; when Bern went Reformed in 1528 and Geneva in 1536, Fribourg chose the other side, expelled or silenced the evangelicals among its own burghers, broke with Geneva over the alliance, and became the chief Catholic power of western Switzerland. It joined the Golden League of the Catholic cantons in 1586, received the Jesuits and gave them its college in 1582, and Peter Canisius spent his last seventeen years there, dying in 1597 and being buried in the church of St Michael. Fribourg's choice meant that the Reformed Vaud and Geneva were never territorially continuous with Reformed Bern, and that the Catholic recovery in Savoy had a base. The dictionary enters Fribourg because a Reformed dictionary should be able to describe a city that heard the Reformation plainly, from its nearest neighbours, and said no, without reducing that to ignorance or corruption.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a league as a confederacy; a college as a society for the pursuit of learning; to silence as to put to silence; and a burgher as an inhabitant of a borough.
webster_full: LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.
COLLEGE, n. A society of men invested with certain powers, engaged in some common pursuit, chiefly of learning.
SILENCE, v. To still; to put to silence; to restrain from speaking or preaching; to prohibit.
BURGHER, n. An inhabitant of a borough or walled town; one who possesses a municipal right.
BORDER, n. The outer edge of anything; the exterior limit of a country or region; a frontier.
scriptures: Joh 6:66
From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.
And when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.
And some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not.
But though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him:
corruption_summary: Swiss city-state between Bern and Geneva which refused the Reformation, expelled its evangelicals, joined the Golden League in 1586, and buried Peter Canisius in 1597.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the assumption that a people who refuse the gospel have not heard it. Fribourg heard it as clearly as any city in Europe, from Bern across the river and Geneva down the lake, with its own burghers preaching it in the 1520s, and the council chose the mass, the alliance with Savoy and eventually the Jesuits. The dictionary holds the choice to have been gravely wrong and declines to explain it away. Scripture shows the same division under the plainest preaching there has ever been: “some believed the things which were spoken, and some believed not” (Act 28:24).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that unbelief under clear preaching is a moral act, not an information problem. Of the Lord's own hearers it is written that “though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him” (Joh 12:37), and of his own disciples that “many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (Joh 6:66). The Athenians' response is the ordinary one and was Fribourg's: “some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter” (Act 17:32).

“though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him” (Joh 12:37) — the Reformation heard from across the river.
“some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter” (Act 17:32) — the Jesuit college given in 1582.

pos: n. (the forest canton that gave Switzerland its name, executed the preacher Jakob Kaiser in 1529, and killed Zwingli at Kappel)
etymology: German Schwyz, of uncertain Germanic root, perhaps from a settler's name; the confederation took its name from this canton.
biblical_def: Schwyz is the canton that gave the confederation its name and fought hardest against its Reformation. One of the three forest cantons of the original league, poor, pastoral and intensely attached to the old religion and to the mercenary service the Reformed preachers denounced, it led the five inner cantons that resisted Zurich. In May 1529 its authorities seized Jakob Kaiser, a Reformed preacher of Zurich's territory taken on Schwyz ground, and burned him at Schwyz for heresy; the execution precipitated the First War of Kappel, which ended in a negotiated peace without a battle. The settlement broke down in 1531 when Zurich put the inner cantons under an embargo on grain, salt and iron, and the five cantons marched: at Kappel on 11 October 1531 Zurich's small force was broken and Zwingli, who had come out with the army as chaplain, was killed on the field and his body afterwards quartered and burned. The Second Peace of Kappel followed, fixing the religious border of Switzerland where it still largely runs. The dictionary enters Schwyz because the Swiss Reformation was halted by armed Catholic peasants who had heard the preaching and wanted none of it, and because Zurich's food embargo was the provocation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an embargo as a restraint on ships or trade; a mercenary as a soldier hired into foreign service; a canton as a small district constituting a state; and a chaplain as a clergyman attached to an army.
webster_full: EMBARGO, n. In commerce, a restraint on ships or merchandise by public authority; a prohibition of departure.
MERCENARY, n. One who is hired; a soldier who is hired into foreign service.
CANTON, n. A small portion or district of territory, constituting a distinct state or government, as in Switzerland.
CHAPLAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the charge of a chapel; a clergyman who belongs to a ship of war or to a regiment.
HALBERD, n. A military weapon consisting of a long staff with a cutting blade and a point at the end.
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
And they said, Lord, behold, here are two swords. And he said unto them, It is enough.
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
corruption_summary: Forest canton that gave Switzerland its name, burned the preacher Jakob Kaiser in 1529, and defeated and killed Zwingli at Kappel in October 1531.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the minister in arms, and Zwingli is the Reformation's most famous instance. He had argued the case for the Zurich embargo, he went out with the troops, and he died in the line at Kappel with a weapon at hand; the dictionary honours his work on the text and his preaching, and judges that he had no business on that field. The Lord's words in the garden are addressed to a disciple defending him: “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52), and Zwingli perished with it within three years of the embargo he urged.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the nature of the kingdom and therefore of its weapons. “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) is the reason given for why the Lord's servants did not fight for him, and the apostolic rule follows from it, that “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4). Schwyz on its side burned a man for preaching, which the dictionary names as murder; and the disciples' two swords were answered by the Lord with “It is enough” (Luk 22:38), which was not an armoury.

“the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4) — Jakob Kaiser burned at Schwyz in May 1529.

pos: n. (the Italian-speaking subject lands south of the Alps, whose Locarno congregation was expelled to Zurich in 1555)
etymology: Italian Ticino, from the river Ticinus; the Swiss cantons held these valleys as subject bailiwicks from the early sixteenth century.
biblical_def: Ticino is the Italian-speaking country south of the Alps which the Swiss cantons governed as conquered territory, and the one place where an Italian Reformed congregation grew up inside the confederation and was destroyed by it. The bailiwicks were administered jointly, which meant that the Catholic inner cantons had a veto; and when Reformed preaching took hold at Locarno in the 1540s under Giovanni Beccaria, a schoolmaster, and a congregation of perhaps two hundred formed, the Catholic cantons demanded its suppression. The federal diet decided in 1555 that the Locarno Protestants must recant or leave. About a hundred and fifty men, women and children went over the Alps in the early winter of 1555, were received at Zurich, were given a church and the right to trade, and their silk-weaving became one of the foundations of Zurich's industry; their descendants include the Orelli and Muralt families. Zurich had voted in the diet and could not save them, which is the bitter part. The dictionary enters Ticino because the Reformed cantons governed subject peoples and governed them badly, and the Locarno exiles are the proof held by the party that benefited.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bailiwick as the jurisdiction of a bailiff; a veto as a refusal to approve; exile as banishment; and a weaver as one whose occupation is weaving.
webster_full: BAILIWICK, n. The precinct in which a bailiff has jurisdiction; the limits of a bailiff's authority.
VETO, n. A forbidding; the exercise of a right to refuse assent to a measure.
EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country by authority.
WEAVER, n. One whose occupation is to weave; one who makes cloth or other textile fabric.
SUBJECT, a. Placed or situate under; being under the power and dominion of another.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
corruption_summary: Italian-speaking subject bailiwicks of the Swiss cantons, whose Locarno congregation was required in 1555 to recant or leave and went over the Alps to Zurich.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the Reformed government of subject peoples, and the dictionary puts the charge on its own side without softening. The Swiss confederation held Ticino as conquered ground administered for the profit of the cantons; its Italian-speaking inhabitants had no vote in the diet that decided their religion; and Protestant Zurich sat in the diet that banished a Protestant congregation because the arrangement required unanimity and Zurich valued the arrangement. The Locarnese were strangers and pilgrims on the earth in the plainest sense, and the apostle's address fits them, “I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pilgrim character of the church, which such an expulsion makes visible rather than creating. “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) was the Locarnese position in the winter of 1555, and of all such companies it is written that they desire “a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:16). The hundred and fifty who crossed the passes belong among those “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38), and their silk looms afterwards enriched the city that had failed to protect them.

pos: n. (the Rhineland province of Strasbourg, where Bucer and Capito built the Reformation's most hospitable city and Calvin learned to pastor)
etymology: French Alsace, German Elsass, from Old High German Ali-saz, the foreign settlement, or Ell-sass, dwellers on the Ill.
biblical_def: Alsace is the Rhineland province whose chief city did more for the Reformation by taking people in than most states did by legislating. Strasbourg, an imperial free city, reformed from 1523 under Matthew Zell, Wolfgang Capito, Caspar Hedio and above all Martin Bucer, who made it the Reformation's great house of mediation: Bucer attended every colloquy, drafted the Tetrapolitan Confession of 1530 with Capito and Hedio for the cities that could sign neither Wittenberg's nor Zurich's formula, and worked for twenty years to reconcile the Lutheran and Swiss doctrines of the Supper. Strasbourg also received everyone: French refugees, Anabaptists, Schwenckfeldians and Spiritualists it tolerated far longer than its neighbours, and John Calvin, expelled from Geneva in 1538, spent three years there pastoring the French congregation, learning Bucer's pattern of psalm-singing, catechising and discipline, and rewriting the Institutes. The Alsatian countryside stayed mixed and largely Lutheran; the Peace of Westphalia gave the province to France in 1648 while guaranteeing its Protestant churches, which is why Lutheran congregations exist in France today. The dictionary enters Alsace because Calvin's Geneva was Bucer's Strasbourg applied with a firmer hand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mediation as interposition between parties at variance; a colloquy as a conference; refuge as shelter from danger; and a liturgy as a form of prayers for public worship.
webster_full: MEDIATION, n. Interposition; intervention; agency between parties at variance, with a view to reconcile them.
COLLOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a conference.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
LITURGY, n. In a general sense, all public ceremonies that belong to divine service; a formulary of public prayers.
RECONCILE, v. To conciliate anew; to call back into union and friendship the affections which have been alienated.
scriptures: Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Rom 15:7
Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Phi 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
corruption_summary: Rhineland province whose city of Strasbourg reformed under Bucer and Capito, framed the Tetrapolitan Confession in 1530, and sheltered Calvin from 1538 to 1541.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the mediating temper that ends in formulas nobody holds, which is the standing charge against Bucer and which the dictionary accepts in part. His Wittenberg Concord of 1536 on the Supper was accepted by both parties because each could read it its own way, and that is not unity but a postponement; the Reformed churches afterwards had to say plainly what they meant. What the dictionary will not grant is that his labour was therefore wasted. “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) is a command, and a man who spends his life at it will sometimes draft an ambiguous sentence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the receiving of brethren, which Strasbourg practised before it was fashionable and at real cost: “Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us” (Rom 15:7). Bucer's congregational order, the psalms in metre, the catechism, the weekly discipline, is the apostolic instruction put into a parish week, that the word of Christ should dwell in them richly, “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). The temper required of it is that “in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves” (Phi 2:3).
